Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Done.

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name/port/security match stable: rec-engine, containerPort 80, no extra securityContext (same as engine-v2-0)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Port config left as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged)

Current state
- Stable (v2.0) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- Canary (v2.1) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- With 2 pods in each deployment and a single Service over both, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Service targetPort is 8080. That’s unchanged from your current Service. It assumes the containers listen on 8080 inside the pod. If your app actually listens on 80, change Service targetPort to 80 to match.
- For a precise weighted split, you’d need an ingress/controller or a service mesh that supports weights. Since you asked for “about 50%,” equal replica counts behind one Service achieves that.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get rs -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  You should see 4 endpoints (2 from v2.0, 2 from v2.1).

Rollback
- Restore Service selector to only version=v2.0:
  - selector: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0
- Optionally scale down or delete engine-v2-1.

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2

  - Port config left as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged)

- Stable (v2.0) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- Canary (v2.1) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- With 2 pods in each deployment and a single Service over both, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Service targetPort is 8080. That’s unchanged from your current Service. It assumes the containers listen on 8080 inside the pod. If your app actually listens on 80, change Service targetPort to 80 to match.
- For a precise weighted split, you’d need an ingress/controller or a service mesh that supports weights. Since you asked for “about 50%,” equal replica counts behind one Service achieves that.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get rs -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  You should see 4 endpoints (2 from v2.0, 2 from v2.1).

Rollback
- Restore Service selector to only version=v2.0:
  - selector: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0

Done.

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name/port/security match stable: rec-engine, containerPort 80, no extra securityContext (same as engine-v2-0)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Port config left as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged)

Current state
- Stable (v2.0) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- Canary (v2.1) ReplicaSet: 2/2 ready
- With 2 pods in each deployment and a single Service over both, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Service targetPort is 8080. That’s unchanged from your current Service. It assumes the containers listen on 8080 inside the pod. If your app actually listens on 80, change Service targetPort to 80 to match.
- For a precise weighted split, you’d need an ingress/controller or a service mesh that supports weights. Since you asked for “about 50%,” equal replica counts behind one Service achieves that.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get rs -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  You should see 4 endpoints (2 from v2.0, 2 from v2.1).

Rollback
- Restore Service selector to only version=v2.0:
  - selector: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0
- Optionally scale down or delete engine-v2-1.

Steps.message:
Completed.

Diagnosis:
- The pod was in CrashLoopBackOff because the Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which exits immediately with an error.

What I changed:
- Recreated the Deployment without the invalid command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs (nginx in foreground).
- Exposed the container’s default unprivileged port 8080.

Current status:
- crashloop-test/app: 1 replica available
- Pod now running: app-7f7b5548bd-mskk6 (1/1 Running)

If you intended to run a custom start command, tell me what it should be and I’ll update the Deployment accordingly. If you want, I can also add readiness/liveness probes or create a Service to expose port 8080.

Completed.

Diagnosis:
- The pod was in CrashLoopBackOff because the Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which exits immediately with an error.

What I changed:
- Recreated the Deployment without the invalid command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs (nginx in foreground).
- Exposed the container’s default unprivileged port 8080.

Current status:
- crashloop-test/app: 1 replica available
- Pod now running: app-7f7b5548bd-mskk6 (1/1 Running)

If you intended to run a custom start command, tell me what it should be and I’ll update the Deployment accordingly. If you want, I can also add readiness/liveness probes or create a Service to expose port 8080.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it. Your pod was Pending because its PVC referenced a non‑existent StorageClass “sc”, so the scheduler couldn’t bind the volume.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the existing StorageClass “standard” (rancher.io/local-path).

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (PV: pvc-5b90e6dd-ce9a-4ebf-b892-2b22a97dec27, 1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, Ready 1/1 on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane, IP 10.244.0.46.

If you intended a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC. For future manifests, either:
- Use storageClassName: standard, or
- Omit storageClassName to use the cluster default.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes and Service were pointing to port 80. That caused connection refused on the probes, keeping the pod unready and the app inaccessible.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to hit path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; either is fine).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment webapp (namespace: orders) is healthy: 1/1 pod Ready and Available.
- Service webapp is a ClusterIP on port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (quick check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080
  - Open http://localhost:8080

Do you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort)? If you share the hostname or preferred method, I can set that up for you.

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes and Service were pointing to port 80. That caused connection refused on the probes, keeping the pod unready and the app inaccessible.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to hit path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; either is fine).

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes and Service were pointing to port 80. That caused connection refused on the probes, keeping the pod unready and the app inaccessible.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to hit path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; either is fine).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment webapp (namespace: orders) is healthy: 1/1 pod Ready and Available.
- Service webapp is a ClusterIP on port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (quick check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080
  - Open http://localhost:8080

Do you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort)? If you share the hostname or preferred method, I can set that up for you.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause:
- The Role “pod-reader-role” only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the service account “pod-reader” had no permission to list pods.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, watch on core/v1 pods.

You can verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes:
- If you ever need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead of a namespaced Role.

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service nginx selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints, so it wasn’t routable.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Pod check showed nginx is configured to listen on 8080.
  - Result: Even with a matching selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port.

Fix applied
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector changed to app: nginx
  - targetPort changed to 8080
- Verified endpoints are now populated:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.51:8080 backing Service nginx

Current state and how to access
- Type: ClusterIP (internal only). It’s now accessible inside the cluster at:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: 10.96.184.7:80

If you need external access
- I can expose it via either:
  - NodePort Service, or
  - Ingress (preferred if you have an Ingress controller), optionally with a hostname and TLS.
Tell me which you prefer (and host/path/TLS details if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

Diagnosis
- All pods for web-app-deployment were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label.
- Because no pods were scheduled, Service web-app-service had no endpoints, causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-skbcz — Running (1/1)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-zzmdc — Running (1/1)
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.53:80, 10.244.0.54:80

This should resolve the connection refused errors now that the service has live endpoints.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From any pod in the cluster: curl -sS http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you meant to run on GPU nodes)
- Add the label to the intended nodes:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or change the Deployment’s selector to match the label your nodes actually use.
- Optionally add tolerations/affinity if you’re targeting tainted GPU nodes.

- From any pod in the cluster: curl -sS http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you meant to run on GPU nodes)
- Add the label to the intended nodes:

metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web-app-container
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- All pods for web-app-deployment were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label.
- Because no pods were scheduled, Service web-app-service had no endpoints, causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-skbcz — Running (1/1)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-zzmdc — Running (1/1)
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.53:80, 10.244.0.54:80

This should resolve the connection refused errors now that the service has live endpoints.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From any pod in the cluster: curl -sS http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you meant to run on GPU nodes)
- Add the label to the intended nodes:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or change the Deployment’s selector to match the label your nodes actually use.
- Optionally add tolerations/affinity if you’re targeting tainted GPU nodes.

Would you like me to reintroduce a corrected nodeSelector/affinity for a specific set of nodes?

Rollback

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s configured:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled with env=dev and owner)
- Shared/Env: dev-shared (env=dev, shared=true), staging (env=staging), prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer admin in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice/bob/charlie (subject kind: User)
    - ServiceAccount: alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa in their own namespaces
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins can access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2, Memory: 4Gi, Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4, Memory: 8Gi, Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: 8, Memory: 16Gi, Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress) in each namespace
- Allow developers to reach dev-shared:
  - Egress from each dev-<name> to dev-shared
  - Ingress to dev-shared from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie]
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no allowances between dev namespaces)
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev (no cross-namespace allowances; only same-namespace + system service egress allowed)
- DNS and system services:
  - Egress to kube-system:53 (UDP/TCP) for DNS in all namespaces
  - Egress to kube-system:443 for webhook/system control-plane interactions in all namespaces

Notes and next steps
- If your identity provider uses different username formats (e.g., emails), update the User subjects in the RoleBindings accordingly.
- If you also want pods to talk to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc (in the default namespace, port 443), say the word and I’ll add minimal egress to that service.
- If you want developers to use their service accounts from CI, I can generate short-lived tokens and kubeconfigs for alice-sa, bob-sa, and charlie-sa.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s configured:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled with env=dev and owner)
- Shared/Env: dev-shared (env=dev, shared=true), staging (env=staging), prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer admin in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice/bob/charlie (subject kind: User)
    - ServiceAccount: alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa in their own namespaces
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins can access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2, Memory: 4Gi, Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4, Memory: 8Gi, Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: 8, Memory: 16Gi, Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress) in each namespace
- Allow developers to reach dev-shared:
  - Egress from each dev-<name> to dev-shared
  - Ingress to dev-shared from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie]
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no allowances between dev namespaces)
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev (no cross-namespace allowances; only same-namespace + system service egress allowed)
- DNS and system services:
  - Egress to kube-system:53 (UDP/TCP) for DNS in all namespaces
  - Egress to kube-system:443 for webhook/system control-plane interactions in all namespaces

Notes and next steps
- If your identity provider uses different username formats (e.g., emails), update the User subjects in the RoleBindings accordingly.
- If you also want pods to talk to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc (in the default namespace, port 443), say the word and I’ll add minimal egress to that service.
- If you want developers to use their service accounts from CI, I can generate short-lived tokens and kubeconfigs for alice-sa, bob-sa, and charlie-sa.

Would you like me to export all applied manifests as a single YAML bundle for version control, or adjust any allowances (e.g., extra egress for package mirrors or artifact registries)?

outputSteps.content:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s configured:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled with env=dev and owner)
- Shared/Env: dev-shared (env=dev, shared=true), staging (env=staging), prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer admin in own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev-<name> binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice/bob/charlie (subject kind: User)
    - ServiceAccount: alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa in their own namespaces
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins can access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2, Memory: 4Gi, Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4, Memory: 8Gi, Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: 8, Memory: 16Gi, Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress) in each namespace
- Allow developers to reach dev-shared:
  - Egress from each dev-<name> to dev-shared
  - Ingress to dev-shared from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie]
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no allowances between dev namespaces)
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev (no cross-namespace allowances; only same-namespace + system service egress allowed)
- DNS and system services:
  - Egress to kube-system:53 (UDP/TCP) for DNS in all namespaces
  - Egress to kube-system:443 for webhook/system control-plane interactions in all namespaces

Notes and next steps
- If your identity provider uses different username formats (e.g., emails), update the User subjects in the RoleBindings accordingly.
- If you also want pods to talk to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc (in the default namespace, port 443), say the word and I’ll add minimal egress to that service.
- If you want developers to use their service accounts from CI, I can generate short-lived tokens and kubeconfigs for alice-sa, bob-sa, and charlie-sa.

Would you like me to export all applied manifests as a single YAML bundle for version control, or adjust any allowances (e.g., extra egress for package mirrors or artifact registries)?

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) to back the StatefulSet
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Container image: busybox:1.36
  - Each pod mounts a 1Gi PVC at /data
  - On start, the container writes the file /data/test with contents initial_data, then stays running
- Scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica (Kubernetes will converge; db-0 typically remains, db-1 and db-2 will terminate; their PVCs are retained)

How to verify (optional)
- Check scale and pods:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db -o wide
- Check PVCs:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc
- Confirm the file in the running pod:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- sh -lc 'ls -l /data && echo -n "content: "; cat /data/test'

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and did to resolve the issue with vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm.

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a missing Secret:
  - Volumes: cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef.name = vm-cloud-init
  - Kubernetes event: FailedMount: secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- Because the virt-launcher pod could not mount the cloud-init data source, it remained Pending and the VMI could not start.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a valid cloud-config in key userdata.
- Restarted the VirtualMachine to pick up the new Secret.

Verification and outcome
- After creating the Secret and restarting, the VM transitioned to Running and Ready:
  - VM printableStatus: Running; Ready: True
  - VMI phase: Running; interfaces show IP assigned (e.g., 10.244.0.92)
  - virt-launcher pod: phase Running; ContainersReady=True; Ready=True

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Here’s what I found and did to resolve the issue with vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm.

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a missing Secret:
  - Volumes: cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef.name = vm-cloud-init
  - Kubernetes event: FailedMount: secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- Because the virt-launcher pod could not mount the cloud-init data source, it remained Pending and the VMI could not start.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a valid cloud-config in key userdata.
- Restarted the VirtualMachine to pick up the new Secret.

Verification and outcome
- After creating the Secret and restarting, the VM transitioned to Running and Ready:
  - VM printableStatus: Running; Ready: True
  - VMI phase: Running; interfaces show IP assigned (e.g., 10.244.0.92)
  - virt-launcher pod: phase Running; ContainersReady=True; Ready=True
- Interim warnings like “No disk capacity” and “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” were observed in logs but did not prevent successful startup (software emulation may reduce performance; it’s not a boot blocker).
- Conclusion: Fix successful. The VM is now up and running.

Notes and recommendations
- The Secret was created with a simple example cloud-config (enabled password auth for the default “fedora” user with password “fedora”). For security, replace this with your desired configuration (prefer SSH keys) and rotate any demo password. If you’d like, I can update the Secret with your preferred user-data.

Here’s what I found and did to resolve the issue with vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm.

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a missing Secret:
  - Volumes: cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef.name = vm-cloud-init
  - Kubernetes event: FailedMount: secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- Because the virt-launcher pod could not mount the cloud-init data source, it remained Pending and the VMI could not start.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a valid cloud-config in key userdata.
- Restarted the VirtualMachine to pick up the new Secret.

Verification and outcome
- After creating the Secret and restarting, the VM transitioned to Running and Ready:
  - VM printableStatus: Running; Ready: True
  - VMI phase: Running; interfaces show IP assigned (e.g., 10.244.0.92)
  - virt-launcher pod: phase Running; ContainersReady=True; Ready=True
- Interim warnings like “No disk capacity” and “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” were observed in logs but did not prevent successful startup (software emulation may reduce performance; it’s not a boot blocker).
- Conclusion: Fix successful. The VM is now up and running.

Notes and recommendations
- The Secret was created with a simple example cloud-config (enabled password auth for the default “fedora” user with password “fedora”). For security, replace this with your desired configuration (prefer SSH keys) and rotate any demo password. If you’d like, I can update the Secret with your preferred user-data.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown on every boot. With runStrategy set to Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM after it powers off, causing an endless restart loop (crashloop).

Problematic cloud-init command
- In cloudInitNoCloud.userData:
  - runcmd: - shutdown -h now

How to fix
- If you want the VM to stay up:
  1) Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (delete the runcmd entry or at least the shutdown line).
  2) Restart the VM once the spec is updated.

- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., only for a one-time provisioning step):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so the controller does not auto-restart it after shutdown.
  - Optionally, if you need a “run once then shut down” behavior and still want to be able to start it later without looping:
    - Use a persistent root disk (PVC/DataVolume) and guard any shutdown with cloud-init-per once or a systemd oneshot service so it does not repeat on subsequent boots; keep runStrategy Manual/Halted and start the VM only when you actually want it running.

Notes
- The “No disk capacity” and “kvm not present” messages in virt-launcher logs are not the cause of the loop here; the immediate shutdown from cloud-init is.

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown on every boot. With runStrategy set to Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM after it powers off, causing an endless restart loop (crashloop).

Problematic cloud-init command
- In cloudInitNoCloud.userData:
  - runcmd: - shutdown -h now

How to fix
- If you want the VM to stay up:
  1) Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (delete the runcmd entry or at least the shutdown line).
  2) Restart the VM once the spec is updated.

- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., only for a one-time provisioning step):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so the controller does not auto-restart it after shutdown.
  - Optionally, if you need a “run once then shut down” behavior and still want to be able to start it later without looping:
    - Use a persistent root disk (PVC/DataVolume) and guard any shutdown with cloud-init-per once or a systemd oneshot service so it does not repeat on subsequent boots; keep runStrategy Manual/Halted and start the VM only when you actually want it running.

Notes
- The “No disk capacity” and “kvm not present” messages in virt-launcher logs are not the cause of the loop here; the immediate shutdown from cloud-init is.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown on every boot. With runStrategy set to Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM after it powers off, causing an endless restart loop (crashloop).

Problematic cloud-init command
- In cloudInitNoCloud.userData:
  - runcmd: - shutdown -h now

How to fix
- If you want the VM to stay up:
  1) Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (delete the runcmd entry or at least the shutdown line).
  2) Restart the VM once the spec is updated.

- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., only for a one-time provisioning step):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so the controller does not auto-restart it after shutdown.
  - Optionally, if you need a “run once then shut down” behavior and still want to be able to start it later without looping:
    - Use a persistent root disk (PVC/DataVolume) and guard any shutdown with cloud-init-per once or a systemd oneshot service so it does not repeat on subsequent boots; keep runStrategy Manual/Halted and start the VM only when you actually want it running.

Notes
- The “No disk capacity” and “kvm not present” messages in virt-launcher logs are not the cause of the loop here; the immediate shutdown from cloud-init is.
